source: Acceleration and Its Sign
a = Δv/Δt; an object slows down when its acceleration points opposite to its velocity.
Students think negative acceleration always means slowing down.
In Acceleration acceleration was how quickly velocity changes. Now velocities carry signs, so acceleration does too, and its sign holds a surprise.

$\role{acceleration}{a} = \dfrac{\role[change in velocity]{velocity}{\Delta v}}{\role[time interval]{time}{\Delta t}} = \dfrac{\role[final velocity]{velocity}{v_f} - \role[initial velocity]{velocity}{v_i}}{\role[time interval]{time}{\Delta t}}$. An object speeds up when $a$ and $v$ point the same way and slows down when they point opposite ways. The sign of $a$ alone doesn't tell you which.

Acceleration points in the direction of the change in velocity. A car moving in the $-x$ direction at $-10\ \text{m/s}$ that speeds up to $-16\ \text{m/s}$ has a change of $-6\ \text{m/s}$: its acceleration is negative and it is speeding up. "Negative" is a direction on your axis, not a word for "slowing".
The cart starts moving left with a steady acceleration to the right: it slows, stops at t = 2 s and speeds up to the right.
Same signs: speeding up. Opposite signs: slowing down.
Worked examples
A bus heading west speeds up from $10\ \text{m/s}$ to $16\ \text{m/s}$ in $3\ \text{s}$. Take east as $+x$.
Speeding up in the minus direction
Heading west, both velocities are negative: $v_i = -10\ \text{m/s}$, $v_f = -16\ \text{m/s}$.
Negative acceleration, and the bus is speeding up, because $a$ and $v$ are both negative.
A ball rolls up a ramp at $+6\ \text{m/s}$. Five seconds later it rolls down at $-4\ \text{m/s}$. Find its acceleration.
Through a turnaround
The ball slowed, stopped for an instant and sped up the other way, with the same acceleration the whole time.

Thinking a negative acceleration always means slowing down. It means slowing down only when the velocity is positive. Check by comparing directions: draw the $v$ arrow and the $a$ arrow. Same way, speeding up; opposite ways, slowing down. The word "deceleration" is fine in everyday talk, but in a problem always write $a$ with its sign.
